explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The LORD says the heifer must be one that “…has never been placed under a yoke.” (Numbers 19:2) So a heifer that's already been put to work is out. This one needs a clean record, and nobody gets to say it pulled a few carts on the side.

False is right, baker. Along with being unblemished with no defect, the heifer has to be red, and it has never been placed under a yoke (Numbers 19:2). So that's a red heifer, a spotless one, and one that has never worked a day under a yoke. Finding that animal is a whole project, and I bet the Israelites wanted it done right.

Right, baker. Eleazar the priest has the heifer brought outside the camp and slaughtered in his presence (Numbers 19:3). The whole thing happens out past the tents. Nobody's doing this one in the middle of the neighborhood.

I see why you'd go there, friend, since the Tent of Meeting is in this passage. But it only comes up later, when the blood is sprinkled toward its front (Numbers 19:4). The heifer itself is brought outside the camp and slaughtered there (Numbers 19:3). It never goes inside.

The text doesn't put the heifer by any altar, baker. It says the heifer is brought outside the camp and slaughtered in the priest's presence (Numbers 19:3). I'll admit I'd have pictured an altar too, since that's where my mind goes when a priest is involved. But this one happens out past the camp, with Eleazar watching.

Seven, baker. Eleazar takes some of the blood on his finger and sprinkles it seven times toward the front of the Tent of Meeting (Numbers 19:4). Same finger, same direction, seven times in a row. That's a lot of sprinkling for one finger.

Three sounds reasonable, friend, but the text says more than that. Eleazar sprinkles the blood seven times toward the front of the Tent of Meeting (Numbers 19:4). I'd have stopped at three and gone to sit down. Seven it is.
Twelve is a big number, baker, and a fine one to remember. But the text says Eleazar sprinkles the blood seven times (Numbers 19:4). That's the count for this job. Twelve would be a little too eager.

explanations.answer: Every part including its hide and dung
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says its hide, its flesh and its blood are burned, along with its dung (Numbers 19:5). Nothing gets set aside for later. The whole heifer goes into the fire.

explanations.answer: Only its fat and its kidneys
explanations.explanation: Those two parts don't appear in this passage, friend. The text lists its hide, its flesh and its blood, along with its dung (Numbers 19:5). It's much more than a couple of pieces. The whole heifer goes into the fire.

explanations.answer: Only its flesh and its bones
explanations.explanation: Close on the flesh, baker, but bones aren't mentioned here. The text says its hide, its flesh and its blood are burned, along with its dung (Numbers 19:5). The hide and the dung are the surprise guests. Nothing is left out.

explanations.answer: Cedar wood with hyssop and scarlet wool
explanations.explanation: You've got it, friend. The priest takes cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet wool and throws them onto the burning heifer (Numbers 19:6). Three things, one fire. That's the full list.

explanations.answer: Olive oil with frankincense and salt
explanations.explanation: Not in this passage, baker. None of those three show up in verse 6. The priest throws cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet wool onto the burning heifer (Numbers 19:6).

explanations.answer: Acacia wood with incense and linen
explanations.explanation: The wood is the part to look at, friend. The text says cedar wood, not acacia, and it adds hyssop and scarlet wool (Numbers 19:6). Incense and linen aren't mentioned here at all. It's an easy list to mix up, so give it another look.

True, baker. The priest washes his clothes and bathes, and he's still ceremonially unclean until evening (Numbers 19:7). The man who burned the heifer does the same and is unclean until evening too (Numbers 19:8). Washing is part of the job, but the evening still has to come.

Close, friend, but both men are still unclean after washing. The text says the priest will be ceremonially unclean until evening (Numbers 19:7). The one who burned the heifer is also unclean until evening (Numbers 19:8). Clean clothes, still waiting on evening.

Purification, baker. The ashes are kept by the congregation of Israel for preparing the water of purification (Numbers 19:9). They aren't used up right away. A ceremonially clean man stores them in a ceremonially clean place outside the camp until they're needed.

Atonement is a big word and a good one, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. The text says the ashes are kept by the congregation for preparing the water of purification (Numbers 19:9). The verse then says this is for purification from sin. I grab the fancy word first when I'm guessing too, so hold onto the plain one here.
A nice word, baker, but not the one in the text. The ashes are kept by the congregation for preparing the water of purification (Numbers 19:9). So the water has a very specific job.

Right, friend. This water is for purification from sin (Numbers 19:9). Look at how the LORD sets it up: a man who is ceremonially clean gathers the ashes and stores them in a ceremonially clean place outside the camp. The congregation of Israel keeps them for preparing the water. It's like setting aside one bowl of crushed peppermint for one batch and nothing else. That bowl has a job, and the verse names the job.

Sickness is an easy guess, friend, since water and cleansing go together in most people's heads. But the text says this is for purification from sin (Numbers 19:9). No illness shows up in that verse at all. I'll stick to guessing cookie flavors.
Mildew is a bathroom problem, friend, and the text doesn't mention it. The LORD says this is for purification from sin (Numbers 19:9). Sin is the answer.

I get the thought, baker, but he doesn't stay clean. The man who gathers up the ashes must also wash his clothes, and he will be ceremonially unclean until evening (Numbers 19:10). So gathering the ashes makes him unclean. Another load of laundry.

False is right, friend. The man who gathered up the ashes must wash his clothes, and he will be ceremonially unclean until evening (Numbers 19:10). He started out clean, and gathering the ashes changed that. Unlike the priest and the man who burned the heifer, this verse mentions only washing his clothes, not bathing (Numbers 19:7-8). Another load of laundry.

explanations.answer: He purifies himself with the water on the third and seventh days
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. He must purify himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day, and then he will be clean (Numbers 19:12). Both days count, so he can't skip the first one. Two days, one cleansing.

explanations.answer: He offers a lamb at the Tent of Meeting on the seventh day
explanations.explanation: No lamb in this one, friend. The text says he must purify himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day (Numbers 19:12). It's all about the water of purification.

explanations.answer: He stays outside the camp for the full month after
explanations.explanation: A month is far longer than the text says, baker. A person who touches a dead body is unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11). He purifies himself with the water on the third and seventh days, and then he will be clean (Numbers 19:12). No month needed.
True, baker. Anyone who touches a human corpse and fails to purify himself defiles the tabernacle of the LORD (Numbers 19:13). So skipping the water has a real cost. His uncleanness stays on him.

Not quite, friend. The text says he defiles the tabernacle of the LORD (Numbers 19:13). Failing to purify himself matters. The water has not been sprinkled on him, and his uncleanness is still on him.

explanations.answer: He must be cut off from Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. That person must be cut off from Israel (Numbers 19:13). He remains unclean, because the water of purification has not been sprinkled on him. It's a serious one.

explanations.answer: He must pay a fine in silver
explanations.explanation: No silver in this passage, friend. The text says that person must be cut off from Israel (Numbers 19:13). The problem is that the water of purification was never sprinkled on him.

explanations.answer: He must burn his own tent
explanations.explanation: The tent does come up in this passage, baker, but not for this. Someone who touches a human corpse and fails to purify himself must be cut off from Israel (Numbers 19:13). A tent matters when someone dies inside it, and then it gets sprinkled (Numbers 19:14, 18).
Not this time, baker. Any open container without a lid fastened on it is unclean (Numbers 19:15). So a container with no lid doesn't stay clean. The lid is the thing to look for.

False is right, friend. When someone dies in a tent, any open container without a lid fastened on it is unclean (Numbers 19:15). Fastened is the key word. A lid sitting loose on top doesn't count, the way a cookie jar lid that's just resting there doesn't keep out a thing. So a lid that's really on is what matters in that tent.

explanations.answer: Touching a human bone or a grave
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Anyone in the open field who touches a human bone or a grave will be unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). Same seven days as touching a body. Bones and graves count too.

explanations.answer: Touching a priest's robe or sash
explanations.explanation: Robes and sashes aren't on this list, friend. The text names a human bone or a grave (Numbers 19:16). Those are the ones that make someone unclean for seven days.

explanations.answer: Touching a foreigner's cart or tent
explanations.explanation: A foreigner is in the statute, baker, but not in this line. The text says the foreigner residing among Israel is covered by it (Numbers 19:10). The open-field list is about touching a human bone or a grave (Numbers 19:16).

Fresh, baker. Some of the ashes go into a jar, and fresh water is poured over them (Numbers 19:17). That's for the purification of the unclean person. Two ingredients, ashes and water. Even I can handle a two-ingredient recipe, and I've scorched plenty of batches.
Salt doesn't show up here, friend. The text says to put some of the ashes in a jar and pour fresh water over them (Numbers 19:17). No extra ingredients.
Warm is a reasonable guess, baker, but the text says something else. Fresh water is poured over the ashes in the jar (Numbers 19:17). It doesn't say anything about heating it.

Not yet, baker. After he purifies the unclean person on the seventh day, the one being cleansed must still wash his clothes and bathe in water (Numbers 19:19). Only that evening is he clean. The sprinkling is one step, and the evening is the last.

False is right, friend. After the seventh day's sprinkling, the person must wash his clothes and bathe in water, and that evening he will be clean (Numbers 19:19). So there's still laundry and a bath between the sprinkling and the finish. Clean comes that evening, not right after the sprinkling.

Unclean, baker! Anything the unclean person touches becomes unclean (Numbers 19:22). And it doesn't stop there, because whoever touches that thing is unclean until evening. Picture a thumb covered in chocolate. It grabs the cookie box, the box is smeared, and the next hand that picks it up is smeared too.
Other way around, friend. The text says anything the unclean person touches will become unclean (Numbers 19:22). No touching makes it holy here.
Cursed is a strong word, baker, and the text doesn't use it. It says anything the unclean person touches will become unclean (Numbers 19:22). The word is unclean.
